scenes.title: A different recovery architecture
scenes.text: This is Asteria X One: a one-metre, non-combustive flight demonstrator built to test a different way of recovering reusable launch vehicles. Instead of asking the vehicle to touch down on narrow landing legs, the system transfers the final capture and energy absorption job to a purpose-built recovery platform.

scenes.title: What the demonstrator must prove
scenes.text: The concept separates two questions. First, can a vehicle align itself with a defined capture volume? Second, can a ground structure safely intercept, centre, decelerate, and retain it? Asteria X One tests those interactions with protected electric lift modules, low test energy, and a mechanically bounded operating envelope.

scenes.title: Vehicle structure and packaging
scenes.text: The vehicle uses a reinforced central body with removable service panels, an avionics bay, protected wiring routes, and a structural spine. Four guarded lift modules sit above the capture belt, where they remain clear of the platform throat during descent. The lower body stays narrow enough to enter the recovery funnel.

scenes.title: Protected electric lift modules
scenes.text: Each electric lift pod is carried by triangulated arms rather than a single cantilever. Guards limit accidental rotor contact, while the open arrangement keeps the propulsion modules inspectable and replaceable. This is demonstrator hardware, not an orbital propulsion system; its purpose is controlled vertical motion and repeatable recovery testing.

scenes.title: The circumferential capture belt
scenes.text: Around the vehicle is a continuous reinforced capture belt. That ring distributes interception loads around the body instead of concentrating them into one landing foot or one small hook. Rounded lead-in surfaces help the platform engage the belt even when the vehicle arrives with a limited lateral or angular error.

scenes.title: The PetalCatch recovery platform
scenes.text: PetalCatch is the matching recovery platform. Four braced masts support a wide funnel-shaped cable web. The upper opening creates a large acquisition region, while the smaller suspended throat guides the vehicle toward the centre. Outriggers and anchor plates widen the platform load path into the floor or foundation.

scenes.title: Approach, sensing, and clearance
scenes.text: During approach, onboard and platform sensors estimate relative position, attitude, descent rate, and capture readiness. The vehicle remains above the web until alignment and clearance checks pass. The platform is passive-safe: its geometry provides basic retention even if active tension control or a noncritical sensor becomes unavailable.

scenes.title: How the vehicle enters the funnel
scenes.text: As the vehicle enters the funnel, four dedicated saddles contact the capture belt. The tendons do not pass through the vehicle. Instead, the sloped web redirects horizontal error toward the centre and transfers vertical load into the masts. The narrow lower body passes through the throat with deliberate clearance.

scenes.title: Load transfer and energy absorption
scenes.text: Capture energy then travels through cables, pulleys, load cells, and replaceable spring-damper cartridges. Multiple sectors share the load, reducing the demand on any single component. Cable payout and damping limit peak acceleration, while load cells record the real force history for comparison with the digital model.

scenes.title: Control and independent safety
scenes.text: A controller outside the descent and fan-wash zone supervises platform sensing, sector loads, and emergency states. An independent safety channel can command shutdown without relying on the main flight computer. The physical emergency stop, guarded wiring, and bounded test area are essential parts of the demonstrator, not decorative details.

scenes.title: Inspection and rapid reset
scenes.text: After capture, the vehicle is secured, power is isolated, and the structure is inspected. The platform tendons and damper cartridges are checked, reset, and returned to their reference tension. The design goal is rapid reuse through modular parts and recorded health data, rather than treating every recovery as a one-off event.

scenes.title: What remains to be proven
scenes.text: What you are seeing is a corrected engineering mockup and simulation-backed demonstrator architecture, not flight-proven orbital hardware. The next evidence must come from printed material coupons, component load tests, instrumented dummy drops, tethered hover trials, and progressively harder capture tests. The system earns credibility only when measured hardware agrees with the model.
